Please improve
yourself.
slides.notes: We will implement an agent that can inspect an account, refund a duplicate charge, and provision access. Then we will instrument and evaluate its work before asking an editor agent to revise its instructions. Pending, Inc. and its accounts are fictional; the Python tools, model requests, traces, and evaluations run in your own project.

slides.title: Your first morning at Pending, Inc.
slides.notes: Pending, Inc. is a teaching setting for a familiar engineering problem: connecting a model to existing application operations. The handbook is an opening illustration. We will build and test a configured starting harness before comparing any revisions.

slides.title: The customer was charged twice.
slides.notes: Read the customer request and ask what the agent must know before issuing a refund. The development fixture contains two captured 4900-cent payments on Acme invoice inv-1. The correct outcome refunds pay-2 once while preserving pay-1 and the other account. The empty tool menu explains what we need to implement; it is an illustration rather than a recorded model failure.

slides.title: Define the account state a correct refund should leave.
slides.notes: Ask someone to name the account fields they would check after this request. We need to identify the correct payment, refund the full amount once, and preserve unrelated state. We will later use partial refunds, duplicate refunds, and false completion claims to test the scorer. A fluent final reply cannot establish these account facts.

slides.title: Your manager has one more request.
slides.notes: We will first make the agent executable and observable. Once we can inspect a run and score its outcome, we can give those same records to an editor agent. It changes instructions and selected workflow settings, while our tested tools and final scorer remain fixed. That lets us compare the proposed procedures under the same conditions.

slides.title: Implement the agent, evaluate it, then test harness changes.
slides.notes: This is the three-hour Pending schedule. Allow 15 minutes at the end for final comparison and discussion. Keep extra implementation detail in worked answers.

slides.title: The executor dispatches the model’s selected action.
slides.notes: For this ticket, the model might choose lookup_invoice, then refund_payment. It returns an action name and arguments. Python decides which function handles that action, and the tool changes the simulated account. The model does not directly mutate the account dictionary.

slides.title: Instructions define how the agent should handle the ticket.
slides.notes: The harness is the code and instructions around the model. It controls the request we send, the actions we allow, and the checks we require. We can revise these pieces while using the same model. In our comparison, the dispatcher and tools stay fixed after we test them.

slides.title: Reading a skill adds its procedure to the conversation.
slides.notes: A saved skill has no effect until the executor supplies it to the model. Here the agent can call read_skill; the returned procedure enters the same conversation as other tool results. Agent Lens lets us check whether the skill was read and what the model did afterward.

slides.title: A stable operation_id prevents a repeated write.
slides.notes: Illustration of simulator.execute after a committed provisioning request. The same operation_id and identical arguments return the stored receipt with replayed=true. slides.title: Check the account and the explanation separately.
slides.notes: The state scorer reads the account after execution and checks facts such as payment identity, refund amount, and duplicate effects. The LLM judge reads the request, actions, and final reply to assess whether the explanation is supported. These can disagree: an agent may do the right work and describe it incorrectly. An unavailable judge response stays missing.

slides.title: Management would like to automate management.
slides.notes: The editor uses the same fixed model, but its request is to revise the harness rather than resolve a customer ticket. We supply the current configuration and a saved execution. The permitted edits are instructions, the verification skill, and bounded workflow rules. Tools and scoring stay fixed so any measured difference concerns the harness we changed.

slides.title: Propose two edits to the same starting harness.
slides.notes: Propose asks the editor for two competing changes, such as clearer verification instructions or a mandatory completion check. A and B start from the same parent. Neither receives the other candidate’s test result at this point. We review their saved configurations before allowing the probes.

slides.title: Run each candidate from the original account state.
slides.notes: If candidate A has already issued a refund, B must not inherit that refunded account. The controller resets the case before each probe. Compare the actions and returned state of both runs; a successful tool response alone does not tell us the ticket was handled correctly.

slides.title: Compare the probe results before selecting a harness.
slides.notes: Compose receives the proposed configurations and both execution records. It can choose A or B, combine parts of them, or retain the parent. Its rationale explains that choice, but the choice still needs an execution. The solid paths show versions; colors identify alternatives rather than scores.

slides.title: Execute the harness returned by the composition decision.
slides.notes: A combination may differ from both tested candidates, so we run the returned configuration as its own probe. A Retain decision also runs through this step without inventing a new executable version. We can then inspect the specific execution associated with the decision.

slides.title: Save the selected harness and a lesson for onboarding.
slides.notes: Reflect asks the editor what it learned from the selected run and where that conclusion may not apply. We keep the lesson with that run, then execute the selected harness on onboarding before proposing more changes. This carried-harness teaching protocol differs from the full upstream Harness² cross-task procedure.

slides.title: Give the editor the starting execution and harness.
slides.notes: Conceptual variable names match the visible controller; actual notebook uses _s,_case,_parent,_prefix,_f. It passes prior_experience from round1 into round2. Ask which input would be inappropriate: final-test scores.

slides.notes: The editor returns a structured harness in its decision. slides.title: Require a passing check of the current state before finish.
slides.notes: The loop stores last_check with passed and the digest of world. With verify_before_finish true, finish is rejected if that check is absent, failed, or no longer matches the current state. This is a runtime completion rule. check_work gives public development feedback; the independent final scorer separately checks entire expected accounts and the required resolution.

slides.title: This candidate required a check before completion.
slides.notes: Recorded candidate B changed verify_before_finish from false to true. It produced the explicit check sequence. Spans: rejected finish 9ed1e7824138ec0e, check_work 2d49d1d8d3ddeb5d, accepted finish 3e19e007d013d4d2. This is a behavior change, not yet evidence of better quality.

slides.title: The next round tests changes to the previous selection.
slides.notes: Recursive self-improvement here means that an agent evaluates executions of a harness, proposes revisions, and later examines work done under the selected revision. The retained lesson supplies context for the next attempt. The language model’s weights never change. Our workshop carries a selected harness between two tasks; the upstream Harness² procedure has a broader recursion and experience-library design.
